Q: Lerna publish adds gitHead key to package.jsons A:

To add some context, and possibly an answer for others who land on this question, here is roughly what Lerna publish does:

  1. Creates the tag commit (e.g. v1.0.0) and pushes that to github.

  2. Adds that commit hash as gitHead to the package.json file of each package marked for publishing (but doesn't commit these changes).

  3. Publishes the packages with that field in them.

  4. Resets the package.json files.

So if everything goes to plan, the packages on npmjs.com will have a gitHead field in their package.json files which points to the exact commit from which they were built, but that field will not be saved the package.json files in your repo as:

  1. It's not needed there.

  2. It will be overwritten (temporarily) during next publish.

  3. It would require an additional commit (it can't happen during the tag commit as it uses that commit's hash).

Where things get funky is when the publish command fails (typically due to authentication or expired tokens) as that kills the command before it gets to the reset step, leaving uncommitted changes in your package.json files.

What you should do at that point is:

1 - Manually publish

Keeping the uncommitted gitHead field changes, manually publish all your changed packages (examine the tagged commit to see which were selected) with npm publish (remember to do this in the package sub directories and not root).

Although gitHead isn't currently required, it's nice to have it there.

2 - Remove gitHead

Remove the gitHead field from your package.json files. You don't need it. In fact you may well find you have an outdated one if you've been through a failure before and committed these temporary fields thinking you had to keep them.

Here is the current source code of the Lerna publish command: https://github.com/lerna/lerna/blob/0be4313641e4757b1b68fe8ac178187d131a9bc4/libs/commands/publish/src/index.ts#L376

Q: Laravel app handling redirects unexpectedly A:

First take the proxy out of the equation and look at what PHP-FPM itself (or whatever you run there) returns, then deal with nginx/Apache:

php -S 127.0.0.1:8080 -t public
curl -si http://127.0.0.1:8080/login/ms

or hit FPM directly with cgi-fcgi, or curl -si the local web server with a Host header, bypassing the proxy.

If you still get 200 with no headers here, it is the code, not the infrastructure. "200, no headers at all, but Symfony's 'Redirecting to…' HTML in the body" means output started before the response was sent: once headers_sent() is true, PHP emits a default 200 and silently drops every header() call, Location and Set-Cookie included.

optimize "fixing" it confirms that: with config and routes cached, Laravel doesn't include those files on every request, so whatever prints something there gets skipped.

Q: Type hint a default return type used unless more specific overload exists A:

I think that the best way to achieve what you want, if you really want to reduce the amount of overload you need, is to do an overload overlap at the cost of a potential type inference error. This is a tradeoff you might accept or not. See the answer from sterliakov for more information: https://stackoverflow.com/a/74567241/6251742

Here is an example that works without numpy installed, your IDE should tell you the return type expected for those two calls, and you can replace whatever you need to fit your usecase:

import typing

type T = str | int


@typing.overload
def foo(  # type: ignore[overload-overlap]
    a: str, b: str, c: str, d: str
) -> str: ...


@typing.overload
def foo(a: T, b: T, c: T, d: T) -> int: ...


def foo(a, b, c, d):
    ...


# If all arguments are of type string, then the revealed type will be str
typing.reveal_type(foo("1", "2", "3", "4"))  # str

# If any of those args are of type int, the result will be int
typing.reveal_type(foo("1", "2", "3", 4))  # int

The ignore comment will silence the typechecker warning about overlap. This overlap is intended, and the ignore won't silence anything else and it won't alter the typechecker ability to infer the correct type.

Q: Docker pull fails with unexpected EOF A:

I was also getting exactly the same error: when Docker Desktop Kubernetes tried to pull images from a private GitLab container registry, it would give the error "Failed to pull image [...] short read: expected [n] bytes but got 0: unexpected EOF" (different n for different images). This started happening after upgrading to Docker Desktop 4.90.0 from a much older version, on MacOS.

Kubernetes was able to pull public images just fine, and the images from the private registry did pull successfully via the docker pull CLI command.

What fixed the problem in the end was spotting the "Choose cluster provisioning method" options under "Cluster settings" in the Kubernetes page of the Docker Desktop settings - it had defaulted to "kind", rather than "Kubeadm". After I switched to "Kubeadm" (resetting the cluster), it all worked as expected.

Q: Manually triggering Stripe payout to connected account fails - not enough balance error despite stripe account being loaded A:

The error is accurate: the connected account's available balance really is zero. The transfers you see as "due" with a date a week ahead are the money in transit – it is on the connected account, but as pending balance until the settlement window passes. A payout can only draw from available, never from pending, so payouts->create will keep failing until that date, no matter what the dashboard shows.

Two things make it worse in your command:

  1. 'source_type' => 'card' limits the payout to the card-funded part of the balance only. Drop it unless you really need it.
  2. You never check the balance before paying out. If you keep manual payouts, do this first:
$balance = $this->stripe->balance->retrieve([], ['stripe_account' => $accountId]);
$availableGbp = collect($balance->available)->firstWhere('currency', 'gbp')->amount ?? 0;
if ($availableGbp < $payoutAmount) { /* skip, retry on next run */ }

But the bigger point is the design. You want "the provider cannot touch the funds until we release them". The clean way to get that in Stripe Connect is separate charges and transfers:

  • Charge the guest on the platform (a plain PaymentIntent, no transfer_data). The money stays on your platform balance.
  • When your hold period ends, create a Transfer to the connected account for that booking (transfer_group = booking id so it reconciles).
  • Leave the connected account's payout schedule on automatic. Stripe pays out whatever becomes available; you never call payouts->create yourself.

The "release" then happens at the transfer, which is the part you control, and you stop fighting the pending/available timing on the connected side.

For testing in sandbox: normal test cards also produce pending funds. Card 4000 0000 0000 0077 settles instantly into available, so you can exercise the payout path without waiting a week.

Docs: Balance object – available vs pending, test card 4000000000000077 bypasses pending balance, separate charges and transfers.

Q: Why does Laravel pingOnFailure() always report failure even when commands succeed? A:

pingOnFailure() only looks at the exit code of the process, after it has finished, inside the same schedule:run. Whatever the command logs is irrelevant.

A failure ping before the command starts, or twice, means schedule:run is being started more than once: two cron lines, cron plus schedule:work, or two servers. Check crontab -l for every user and your supervisor configs, keep one runner.

The scheduler is single-threaded: due commands run one after another in the same minute, so a long one delays the rest. Spread them out in time or mark the long ones runInBackground().

withoutOverlapping() is a cache mutex with a 24h expiry. If a run gets killed hard, the mutex stays and the command is silently skipped until schedule:clear-cache.

To see the real exit code and error output, add ->appendOutputTo(storage_path('logs/app-test.log')).
